title: Mannheim water capacity limits and development approvals
subtitle: Wilmot water-taking policy referred, groundwater protection study, curbside waste by-law, bulky item review, Victoria Street expropriation
overview: The committee spent most of the afternoon on the water capacity constraint in the Mannheim service area. After a long series of delegations from construction, engineering and development firms, it recommended that staff work with area municipalities on a risk-based approach to allocate up to half of the new capacity expected within five years, and develop an enhanced water conservation program {{vote:m13}}. This matters to residents because stalled development approvals affect housing supply and local jobs, while staff say the system is already drawing more water than it can sustainably supply.

The committee did not decide the 1980 Wilmot water-taking policy. It referred the item, with a motion to suspend rather than rescind the policy, to the February 25 Council meeting {{vote:m8}}. It also recommended a staff report on protecting groundwater and wetlands, to come back alongside the 2027 Water Supply Strategy {{vote:m9}}. Separately, a councillor directed staff, without a motion, to respond to public statements made by delegates and bring clarifying information to Council at the end of February.

The committee also recommended endorsing the Wellesley water and wastewater master plan, adopting a new waste by-law effective March 2, 2026, starting expropriation for Victoria Street South improvements, and studying bulky item collection frequency.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff work with area municipalities on a risk-based approach to allocate up to fifty per cent of capacity coming online within five years, and develop an enhanced water conservation program {{vote:m13}}.

The committee referred the item, including a motion to temporarily suspend the 1980 policy with added public reporting and clarifications, to the February 25 Council meeting {{vote:m8}}; the staff recommendation to rescind was not considered.

The committee recommended that staff report back, alongside the 2027 Water Supply Strategy or sooner, on tools to protect groundwater recharge areas, wetlands and moraine lands, including advocacy for a provincial "Bluebelt" framework {{vote:m9}}.
The committee recommended repealing By-Law 17-007 and approving a new Waste By-law, effective March 2, 2026, to reflect cart-based collection {{vote:m4}}.
The committee recommended that staff study alternative bulky item collection frequencies and report back by September 2026, including information on the Christmas tree program {{vote:m12}}.

decisions.item: Wellesley water and wastewater master plan
decisions.detail: The committee recommended endorsing the final Wellesley master plan and posting it for a 30-day public review {{vote:m3}}.

The committee recommended authorizing the Regional Solicitor to begin expropriation of land and easements for road improvements between Lawrence Avenue and Fischer-Hallman Road in Kitchener {{vote:m5}}.

debate: Delegates from construction, engineering, real estate and development firms said the pause on approvals is cutting work, risking layoffs and driving investment elsewhere. They argued approvals do not mean immediate water use because projects take years to build, and asked for a clear interim framework and seats on the region's working group.

One hydrogeology delegate argued the problem is treatment and operations rather than a groundwater shortage, and that the new safety buffer should be phased in. Staff replied that the region is already operating at a deficit, that demand exceeds sustainable operating capacity, and that water levels around the Mannheim wells are declining and nearing permit trigger levels.

Environmental delegates urged protection of the Waterloo Moraine and recharge areas and supported the groundwater motion. They also objected that rescinding the Wilmot policy had no public consultation. Staff said the Wilmot aquifer holds more water and has long-term monitoring and a private-well complaint process.

On the Wilmot motion, a councillor questioned whether monitoring private wells falls outside the region's authority. Staff noted that water allocated to growth cannot be taken back, so the item was referred to allow the wording to be reviewed.

On groundwater, staff said the requested work is master-plan scale and fits best after the Water Supply Strategy, which led to a change in timing. On bulky items, staff said fixed contract costs limit savings, and councillors debated whether a September report would avoid lame-duck restrictions.
